questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I love the city of Berlin and have had a dream of living here for a long time. The Erasmus program was a good opportunity to live in the city while having something meaningful to do i.e. studying. I also wanted to explore German culture, language and literature more, as it is a big part of my studies in Denmark.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: We were oriented very well per email by the earsmus team at Fu before arrival and afterwards there were several orientation meetings and days, so I will say I was well informed.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: As said above there was orientation days and also information sent out by email. There is also a portal called Distributed Campus where you can find a lot of information. The erasmus team also held a meet-up on one of the first days, where we got to meet other erasmus students which was really nice.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It is hard to find accommodation in Berlin, but not as hard as everyone says. I found a place through my network for the first 6 weeks and from there I could search for a new place on WG-Gesucht and other online platforms. You have to write to a lot of people and be active, but that definitely pays off. I got a very nice room in a WG with three other girls who all turned into close friends. 
It is way easier to find something if you are in town, so I recommend going here even if you haven't found anything yet. People like that they can meet you in person before letting you live at their place :)

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is more expensive, but for me it was totally worth it. You get to live inside the city instead of 1 hour by public transportation from everything. You can be lucky to live with German people or even people from Berlin and not just other exchange students. For me it was also important to find a WG with people around my age (27), because most people in the dorms are 20-21 and have other priorities.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: To be honest the registration is a mess. You can choose courses from your own specific program online and if you want courses from other programs, you have to write to the professor personally in order to get allowance. The first couple of weeks function as some kind of trial period, which is nice, but also very stressful. It is also a jungle to find out how many ECTS you can obtain from each class and if you can even be approved for it. All in all the course registration is a parade of German bureaucracy and makes little sense.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Everyone is trying their best to help and there was a lot of emails back and forth woth professors, coordinators and so on. But after all, you have to do a lot of reseach and work yourself

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got into all the classes I wanted, and my impression is that everyone I know had the same experience. They make it sound harder to get into a class than it is. But I wasn't that satisfied with my classes, so I wish I tried out even more different ones before deciding.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: You can do almost whatever you want, as long as you have the professor's consent. I'm a literature student, but did most of my courses in the North American Institute (JFKI) and even one at anthropology. My advice is to show up to more classes than you are planning to follow, just to feel the vibe and see how big the workload is. I experienced a big different between classes with the same amount of ECTS. Also, most professors will allow you to get more ECTS than said on the syllabus if you do some kind of extra work. This can be very helpful if you need a specific amount for your learning agreement.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I was only allowed to take MA-level courses by my home university, so this is what I did

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: For most of the courses the style of teaching was way more loose and unorganized than at UCPH. The seminars are 1,5 hours and with no break. This was hard for me in the beginning. I didn't like that the discussions weren't very structured and for most of my courses there was no group work, which made it hard for me to participate in class discussions beacuse I get too nervous. But the overall level was mostly the same and the professors were nice and very knowledgable.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Political Depression and the Aesthetics of Sovereignty II
Narratives of Home in North American Literatures
Sites of Labor: Factory, Plantation, Office, Household
Ambivalent Substances: Engaging elements in life-death worlds

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: None of the courses I took will be offered again (I think), but I especially liked Dr. Freire de Andrade Neves as a professor at the anthropology department. I think he will be doing other courses in the future, so check that out :)

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: After some months you will get a message from your phone operator that you have to pay for every MB data used beacuse you spent more data outside DK than inside in the last 4 months. This made me panic and I considered getting a German number, but it turned out that it wasn't bad at all and the price was max 50kr higher a month.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Eating out is so cheap! Transportation is expensive, but we get a discount through the student ticket. In general the student discounts are very good, often half price at museums etc. This was a nice surprise. Housing is pretty expensive but it is possible to find something affordable. And the entrance for clubs is expensive! Often 25 euro, around 200 dkk.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: all kinds of sports classes, different social clubs and a few student parties. I didn't really participate in any of them, but I only heard good things from others

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I participated in the German Vorkurs - a 6 week German course before the semester begins. This was a very nice way to meet people and ease into life in Berlin before starting the acedemic semester, so I definitely recommend that.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Sooo much to do! Of course there is the club culture, but you probably already know about that. Every first sunday in the month, there is Museumssontag, where most museums have free entrance. On sundays there's also the fleamarkets, which is a nice activity. I recommend the one called Nowkölln at Maybachufer. Going for walks in different areas is a very nice activity in Berlin beacuse there's so much life in the streets and coffee or food stops are very affordable. I also went on a few canal tours, which was fun,  and swimming in the lakes is definitely recommended! Krumme Lanke is not that far from campus, so bringing your bathing suit to class and going after is a life hack! 
Theater, concerts and cultural activities in general are often pretty cheap for students, so this is definitely worth checking out. 
Almost every piece of pavement in Berlin has a historical meaning, so there's so much to explore if you're interested in history, WW2, east/west division, art scene etc.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy as it is very similar to Denmark

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Honestly, it was pretty hard to socialize. I guess it is easier if you are better at German than I was

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: A loooot of bureaucracy makes it very frustrating to be in Germany sometimes. Luckily you can laugh about it with the Germans, they hate it too. People are a bit more closed than in DK and not as friendly, but it is not a big problem. I think the city is just bigger and I never had any bad experiences

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I really appreciate the going out culture, how people hang out at cafes, bars, restaurants, small squares and patches of grass all the time. That is something missing in DK, I think. I also like that, despite the stereotype, everything is not so controlled and managed here. Buildings are left, there's more 'wild' nature in the city and more diversity in people

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
You have to bear with the bureaucracy, but people are generally good at helping and they know, that is it very hard to figure out. 
Don't be scared that campus is a bit far from everything. The atmosphere is nice and it is close to nature, lakes and has good libraries, outside areas etc.
It is nice to know just a little bit of German before going. I started from scratch at an evening course once a week for half a year and then did the Vorkurs. This was very helpful both at campus and in general. But campus is pretty international and you can communicate perfectly fine with English

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The student cafe called Pi is nice! Has a rooftop terrace and cheap coffee

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Just living in Berlin, feeling at home here, meeting a lot of different people with different backgrounds. I loved the city before I came here and now I just love it even more. One of the best things is that beacuse everything is cheaper it is so much easier to do stuff, eat out, have another coffee etc. There's so much life here and so much to do so it just feels like a buffet of cool experiences and people

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: University was a bit lonely because it was hard for me to get to know people in my courses. This didn't bother me so much, though, because I had friends elsewhere and I think it is different for everyone

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
